all.title: Playbook branch executor implements 6 of the 9 step types its own validator accepts — update_record, check_knowledge and read_reference are silently skipped
all.evidence: Three sources, read directly. (a) supabase/functions/playbook-execute/index.ts:212-216 — `const BRANCH_ALLOWED = new Set(['instruction','checklist','wait','log_activity','update_record','connector_action','guardrail_check','check_knowledge','read_reference'])` = 9 keys, enforced by validateBranch at L254. (b) The executor for branch steps, `runBranchStep` at L938-1003 (nested inside executeDefinitionSteps), switches on only 6: AST switch-case extraction reports `playbook-execute:947 switch(bs.key) cases=6 default=true -> instruction checklist wait log_activity guardrail_check connector_action`. (c) Its default clause, L998-1001: `bs.status = 'skipped'; bs.at = now(); bs.detail = `skipped: "${bs.key}" not executed in branch preview path`;` — status 'skipped', the run is NOT failed. Set difference: update_record, check_knowledge, read_reference pass validation and are then dropped. `wait` is worse-shaped still — it has a case (L960-964) that hard-codes `bs.status = 'skipped'`. The browser side offers a tenth: src/lib/playbookBuilderApi.ts:66-70 `BRANCH_PRIMITIVES` adds `consult_specialist`, which L160-162 of the same file declares RETIRED.
all.why_it_matters: An owner builds a playbook with a decision step — "if the invoice is overdue, mark the record and check the knowledge base" — the builder offers those steps inside the branch, the server accepts the playbook as valid, it publishes, it runs, and it reports COMPLETED having done neither. The builder already carries a loud warning about this exact failure mode (LivePlaybookBuilder.tsx:1931-1942: "the playbook reports completed having done nothing"), but that safety net only catches step types missing from the registry — these three are IN the registry, so nothing flags them. This is the one finding here that can produce a wrong business outcome rather than just slow work down.

all.title: connector-hub's four-method adapter contract is honoured 280 times and enforced by nothing — the dispatch map is `Record<string, any>` and tsc never sees the file
all.evidence: supabase/functions/connector-hub/index.ts declares 19 interfaces (grep '^interface|^export interface|^type ' — HubItem, AdapterResult, TestResult, SyncDoc, SyncResult, Ctx, McpToolDef, ActionRenderResult, ActionRunResult, NativeAction, TemplateExec, TemplateOpResult, IngestFilters, Candidate, ActionDefRow, LearnedRender, ActionRenderOutcome, OpParams, OpTranslator). None of them describes an adapter. The dispatch map at L6294-6306 is preceded by `// deno-lint-ignore no-explicit-any` and typed `const adapters: Record<string, any>`; the selection at L6307-6308 carries the same suppression (`grep -c no-explicit-any` = 2). Meanwhile the AST tally shows all 70 object-literal adapters implement test/search/fetchRecord/listRecent — a real 4-method contract, 280 implementations, zero declarations. And tsconfig.json has `"include": ["src"]` with no reference to supabase, so the whole directory is outside `tsc` (the same tsconfig also sets `"strict": false`).
all.why_it_matters: Adding the 75th connector is the most common change this file will ever see, and the one thing that would make it safe — "here is the shape an adapter must have" — is written down nowhere the compiler can read. A misspelled `fetchRecord` ships green and fails in production for one provider, in one tenant, on the first fetch. Declaring the interface and typing the map is a small change that converts a runtime class of failure into a build-time one.

all.title: connector-hub's 1,268-line request handler is the accidental half of the file, with a 332-line execute_action branch inside it
all.evidence: AST composition of supabase/functions/connector-hub/index.ts (7,375 lines, 233 top-level statements): provider adapter objects 74 = 2,894 lines; native action packages (*Actions) 20 = 938 lines; PROVIDER_OP_TRANSLATORS = 391 lines; serve() handler = 1,268 lines; everything else = 1,205 lines; remainder ~679 lines of top-level comments and blanks. The serve handler at L6108-7375 is the codebase's 2nd-longest function. Its action branches, measured individually: execute_action L7036-7367 = 332, sync L6869-6979 = 111, sync_business_records = 95, sync_mcp_tools = 91, category_op = 70, sync_financials = 48, template_dry_run = 43, preview_action = 42, sync_ledger = 38, reconcile_financials = 34, search/fetch/list = 31, discover = 29, health_check = 9, test = 7 — about 980 lines of branches, leaving ~288 lines of shared preamble (auth, tenant resolution, feature gate, secret load, template resolution, adapter selection, audit/health/access closures). The 1,205 lines of "everything else" hold at least four distinct subsystems: the declarative template engine (templateAuthHeaders 100, runTemplateOp 114, templateAdapter 28, resolveTemplate), the action-definition registry (resolveActionDefinition 60, renderRegisteredAction 39, runRegisteredAction 88, renderLearnedHttp 52), OAuth/token acquisition (googleAccessToken 27, oauthAccessToken 24, zohoToken 26, fhirBackendToken 24, clientCredsToken, nsAuthHeader 21), and binary file→text extraction (pdfBytesToText, sharepointFetchText 21, gdriveFetchText 23, boxFileText, dropboxFileText).
all.why_it_matters: The honest read on this file is that 4,223 of its 7,375 lines (57%) are per-provider data and should stay exactly where they are — one block per connected system is the right shape and splitting it would make things worse. The debt is the other half: a single function that authenticates, gates features, resolves credentials, picks an adapter and then dispatches sixteen unrelated operations, with the most safety-critical one (execute_action, which actually writes to a customer's live system) buried 900 lines in. That is where reviewers get lost and where the file resists being reasoned about.

all.title: executeDefinitionSteps is the longest function in the codebase at 1,389 lines, and ~161 lines of nested closures are what prevent splitting it
all.evidence: Codebase-wide AST scan of 7,800 functions across 295 files ranks supabase/functions/playbook-execute/index.ts:811 `executeDefinitionSteps` first at 1,389 lines. It is 81% switch: the dispatch at L1052-2180 spans 1,129 lines with 19 cases plus default, case bodies totalling 1,032 (largest: connector_action 259, generate_invoice 124, agentic_step 116, start_onboarding 76, read_reference 75). The residue is four nested closures that capture `run`, `ctx`, `admin` and `tenantId` from the enclosing scope: runBranchStep L938-1003 (66), execRegisteredAction L866-933 (68), resolveRunDeId L833-850 (18), stepAudit L818-826 (9) = 161 lines. That is why it grew to 1,389 lines rather than being broken up along the way, and it is also why the second half-implementation of branch semantics (the top finding) appeared instead of delegation. Sizing note: the switch itself is fine and should survive any restructuring.

all.title: The 19-step-type contract is hand-maintained in five places across the browser/edge boundary with no automated gate
all.evidence: AST extraction of every site. Edge: playbook-execute/index.ts:171 `PRIMITIVES` array = 19 keys; :300 validation switch = 18 cases (omits check_account, no default); :947 branch switch = 6 cases; :1052 dispatch switch = 19 cases + default. Browser: src/lib/playbookBuilderApi.ts:81 `PRIMITIVE_REGISTRY` = 19 entries; src/pages/tenant/systems/LivePlaybookBuilder.tsx:102 `StepParamsEditor` switch = 15 cases + default. I diffed the two 19-key lists: `in EDGE not in REGISTRY: (none)` / `in REGISTRY not in EDGE: (none)` — they agree today. The UI switch carries one case (`consult_specialist`) present in neither list. No `contract-parity` script covers these: grep for contract-parity/contractParity/CONTRACT_PARITY across the repo returns exactly one file, docs/45-certification-scoreboard.md, and no script in scripts/ matches.
all.why_it_matters: Adding or renaming a step type means editing five hand-maintained lists in two languages on two sides of a network boundary. They happen to agree right now, which is luck plus discipline, not a mechanism. The failure mode when they stop agreeing is the same silent one as the branch finding: a playbook validates, publishes, runs, and reports success while skipping work. This is the cheapest defence to add and it protects the highest-consequence contract in the runtime.

all.title: Worst signature in the codebase is 17 positional parameters (runLoop), not the 16 of dispatchTool — and both sit in files tsc never checks
all.evidence: Codebase-wide AST parameter sweep, 7,802 functions / 295 files. Ranking: supabase/functions/agentic-step-execute/index.ts:260 `runLoop` = 17 (admin, tenantId, runId, goal, deName, model, escalationModel, escalationThreshold, tools, policy, deId, contextDocuments, charter, playbookRunId, onGate, stepIndex, entityRef); supabase/functions/de-work/index.ts:548 `dispatchTool` = 16, declared on a single 617-character line; supabase/functions/_shared/guardrailAdjudicator.ts:324 `logAdjudication` = 11; then a cliff to supabase/functions/eval-run/index.ts:454 `auditCompletion` = 8. Each of the top two has exactly ONE call site — runLoop at agentic-step-execute:539-545, dispatchTool at de-work:1450. Both contain runs of three adjacent same-typed parameters: runLoop's `contextDocuments = '', charter = '', playbookRunId = ''` are all defaulted strings; dispatchTool's `entityName?: string|null, ctxAccountForContacts?: string|null, caseEntityRef?: string|null` are all nullable strings, and de-work:1450 fills them positionally with `entityName, contactsFor, entityRef`. tsconfig.json includes only "src", so neither file is type-checked at all.
all.why_it_matters: To answer the question as asked: dispatchTool is not typical and it is not the worst — 99.4% of this codebase's functions take three parameters or fewer, and only two functions exceed eleven. So this is a localized wart, not a house style. It still deserves fixing because in both cases three neighbouring arguments have the same type, so transposing two of them compiles clean, and these are precisely the files the type checker is configured to ignore. With one call site each, converting both to a named-options object is an afternoon.

all.title: connector-hub carries a private copy of PDF extraction that dropped the 15 MB size cap the shared version enforces
all.evidence: supabase/functions/_shared/pdfExtract.ts:12-16 defines `pdfToText`, and :10 exports `MAX_PDF_BYTES = 15 * 1024 * 1024`. Its own header (L2-4) says it was "Extracted from extract-document so the automated/dispatch ingestion paths (demo-ingest, connector-driven ingestion) can handle PDFs too" — i.e. it was extracted for connector-hub. connector-hub/index.ts:1755-1761 nonetheless defines `pdfBytesToText`, whose three-line body is identical to the shared function apart from a try/catch. Both other consumers import the shared one and enforce the cap: extract-document/index.ts:18,66,89 and knowledge-ingest-drain/index.ts:37,166-170 (`if (buf.byteLength > MAX_PDF_BYTES) throw ...`). connector-hub's five PDF call sites — L1952, L1957, L2055, L2825, L5436 — apply only a post-extraction `.slice(0, MAX_DOC_CHARS)`, with no byte-size check before decoding.
all.why_it_matters: A twin copy inside a giant that has already drifted on a resource limit — the exact pattern this codebase has been bitten by before. A large PDF sitting in a customer's SharePoint, Drive, Box or Dropbox gets fully decoded in an edge function with no ceiling, where every other path in the system would have refused it. The fix is one import and one guard, and it also deletes seven lines from the biggest file.

all.title: The escalation rules that decide "stop, get a human" are hand-copied into two of the three paths that enforce them — and the shared loader built for exactly this job is used by only one
all.evidence:
`supabase/functions/_shared/escalation.ts:81` exports `loadEscalationRuleset(admin, tenantId, deId)`, documented at line 78-80 as: "Shared by every enforcement path so they all read the same rules."

`grep -rn "loadEscalationRuleset" src/ supabase/functions/` returns only THREE lines — the definition, plus one import and one call, both in `de-work/index.ts:30` and `:1210`. No other caller exists.

Meanwhile `de-answer/index.ts:512-535` and `widget-ask/index.ts:251-274` each contain a 24-line inline re-implementation. My clone detector flagged them as a 17-line exact match. Reading both: they issue the identical `admin.rpc('resolve_de_escalation', ...)` + `admin.from('de_escalation_rules').select('custom_rules, de_id')` pair, then build the same four-field `EscRuleset` ({frustration_threshold, always_escalate_topics, de_rules, tenant_rules}). The ONLY differences are the autonomy `p_action_type` string ('answer_dock' vs 'answer_widget') and a comment. Both files DO import `evaluateEscalation` from the shared module (`de-answer:31`, `widget-ask:36`) — so the evaluator half is shared and the loader half is copied.
all.why_it_matters: This is the mechanism that pulls a human in when an AI employee is out of its depth. There are three doorways into it and only one uses the shared lock; the other two have their own copies of the same lock, filed by hand. Change the rules in the shared place — add a signal, fix how tenant-wide defaults merge with per-employee ones — and the change reaches the work queue but silently does NOT reach the support chat dock or the website widget, which are the two paths a customer actually touches. Nothing errors; escalation just quietly keeps using the old logic on the customer-facing surfaces. This also qualifies a claim already on record that the answer paths were consolidated: the evaluator was consolidated, the loader was not.

all.title: The permission check that decides which tenant a caller may write to is copy-pasted verbatim into four editing functions
all.why_it_matters: This block answers "who is calling, and whose data may they touch" — the boundary that keeps one customer's data away from another's. It exists as four separate hand-written copies. Six of the 36 functions that accept the internal dispatch secret don't use the shared tenant resolver at all. A tightening applied to one copy — a new check, a stricter fallback — leaves three copies at the old standard, and there is no test comparing them. The four affected functions are the ones that create and amend playbooks and business records, so they are exactly the write paths where a boundary slip would matter most. Note this code is not type-checked either: tsc excludes supabase/functions, so a divergence here has no compiler catching it.

all.title: The website-widget login key is hashed by three separate hand-written copies of the same function
all.evidence:
`grep -rn "function sha256Hex" src/ supabase/functions/` returns three definitions: `src/lib/widgetApi.ts:36`, `supabase/functions/voice-relay/index.ts:35`, `supabase/functions/widget-ask/index.ts:70`.

They are already textually divergent — the browser copy builds the byte array with `Array.from(new Uint8Array(buf))`, both edge copies use `[...new Uint8Array(buf)]`. (Same result today; different code.)

This is the credential contract, not a utility. `src/lib/widgetApi.ts:47` computes `const key_hash = await sha256Hex(plaintext)` and stores it (`:50`). The edge copies compute the hash to look the key back up: `widget-ask:133,150,177` and `voice-relay:86`, each feeding `.from('widget_keys').select(...).eq('key_hash', keyHash).eq('active', true)`.

Because the function is only 3 lines, it is BELOW my 8-line detection window — no line-based tool in this repo would ever flag it.
all.why_it_matters: One side mints the key customers embed on their website; two other sides verify it. All three must hash identically forever, and nothing enforces that — not the parity test, not the type checker (edge code is excluded from tsc), not a shared module. If anyone ever changes the hashing (adds a salt, moves to SHA-512, trims differently), whichever copies they miss stop recognising valid keys: every embedded chat widget and voice line on that tenant's site goes dead with an auth failure, not an error message. The three copies have already drifted in style, which is how they drift in substance later.

all.title: The parity test guards the two twin files but only asserts 4 of their ~14 shared exports — the rest are unwatched twins
all.evidence:
`tests/contract-parity.test.ts` compares exactly: `CATEGORIES`, `CATEGORY_OPS`, `CATEGORY_LABELS`, `AUTH_TYPES`, plus behavioral checks on `isFrameworkPlaceholder`, `dateValues`, `renderTemplate`, and `validateAdapterDefinition` (two fixtures).

`grep -n "^export"` on both copies shows these symbols exist in BOTH trees but are never asserted:
- categoryContracts: `getCategoryOp` (src:126 / edge:122), `legalOps` (src:130 / edge:126), `MAPPABLE_FIELDS` (src:146 / edge:148), `computeHealth` (src:159 / edge:153), `HEALTH_LABELS` (src:171 / edge:165)
- adapterTemplates: `AUTH_META` (:30 both), `validateActionBinding` (:270 both), `walkPath` (:367 both), `renderBody` (:400 both), `renderAction` (src:428 / edge:429)

I diffed `computeHealth` directly (src:159-169 vs edge:153-163) — byte-identical today, including the thresholds `failures >= 3 → 'down'`, `failures >= 1 → 'degraded'`. My detector independently flagged this pair as a 17-line clone (`src/lib/categoryContracts.ts:157-175` ≡ `_shared/categoryContracts.ts:151-169`) and `legalOps` as a 15-line clone.
all.why_it_matters: The safety net is real but smaller than it looks — it covers the vocabulary lists and skips most of the behavior. `computeHealth` is the clearest example: it decides whether a customer's connected system is shown as healthy, degraded, or down. Two identical copies, zero assertions. If the screen's copy and the engine's copy ever disagree on the failure threshold, the dashboard says a connection is fine while the engine has already given up on it — the exact class of lie this repo has been burned by before. This is the cheapest fix on the list: the test file already imports both copies, so covering the remaining exports is added assertions, not new machinery.

all.title: 55 of 60 edge functions hand-roll their own CORS block and 23 hand-roll their own json() helper — there is no shared HTTP module at all
all.evidence:
`grep -rln "const CORS" supabase/functions/ | wc -l` = 55, against `ls supabase/functions/*/index.ts | wc -l` = 60.
`grep -rln "const json = (body" supabase/functions/ | wc -l` = 23.
`ls supabase/functions/_shared/ | grep -i "cors|http|response"` returns nothing, and `grep -rn "Access-Control-Allow-Origin" supabase/functions/_shared/` returns nothing — despite 35 other modules living in `_shared/`.

This is my detector's single most-copied block: 7 exact copies of the same 8 lines (`connector-hub:95-103`, `connector-zendesk:28-36`, `eval-run:30-38`, `invite-team-member:39-47`, `playbook-execute:103-111`, `specialist-consult:66-74`, `verify-domain:49-57`), plus a 6-copy import+CORS variant.

The copies have already drifted. Tallying the method line across all copies:
```
33  'Access-Control-Allow-Methods': 'POST, OPTIONS',
 2  "Access-Control-Allow-Methods": "POST, OPTIONS",   <- different quote style
 1  'GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS',
 1  'GET, POST, OPTIONS',
 1  'GET, OPTIONS',
```
Total footprint measured by summing each file's CORS block plus json() helper: ~304 lines.
all.why_it_matters: Every one of the 60 server functions re-declares which websites are allowed to call it and what an error response looks like. That is ~300 lines of pure ceremony, and more importantly it means a browser-access policy change is a 55-file edit rather than a one-file edit. Today all copies allow all origins ('*'), so the day someone needs to restrict that — a security review, an enterprise customer asking who can call the API — it becomes a 55-file sweep where missing one leaves a door open. The five files that already differ show the copies do drift in practice. This is low-risk to fix and it is the biggest single line-count win available, but it buys tidiness and future agility, not correctness today.

all.title: Three different functions are all named renderTemplate, and one is a silent partial copy of another's placeholder vocabulary
all.evidence:
`grep -rn "function renderTemplate" src/ supabase/functions/` finds four definitions — the guarded twin pair plus two independents:
- `_shared/adapterTemplates.ts:387` — `renderTemplate(tpl, values, urlEncode)` → `{out, missing}`, uses single-brace `{key}` placeholders
- `playbook-execute/index.ts:620` — `renderTemplate(t, ctx, runId, steps?)` → string, uses mustache `{{token}}`, and handles `account.name`, `invoice.amount`, `run.id`, `event.ref`, `event.note`, `invoice.external_ref`, `party.*`
- `onboarding-verify/index.ts:59` — `renderTemplate(tpl, accountName)` → string, body is one line: `tpl.replace(/\{\{account\.name\}\}/g, accountName).trim()`

The last is a strict subset of playbook-execute's token set: it recognises `{{account.name}}` and nothing else, silently leaving every other mustache token as literal text in the output.
all.why_it_matters: Two hazards in one name. First, three functions with the same name and three different signatures means anyone reading or grepping this code can easily reason about the wrong one — and the one in the guarded twin file is guarded, so a reader who checks 'is renderTemplate protected?' gets a misleading yes. Second and concretely: `onboarding-verify` understands exactly one placeholder. When someone adds a token to the playbook renderer, any template that flows through onboarding verification renders it as raw `{{invoice.amount}}` text rather than a number — no error, just a broken-looking message in front of a brand-new customer during onboarding, which is the worst possible audience for it.

all.title: connector-hub re-implements the adapter request-rendering pipeline that _shared/renderAction already performs
all.evidence:
My detector flagged a 3-copy cross-tree group: `src/lib/adapterTemplates.ts:434-442` ≡ `supabase/functions/_shared/adapterTemplates.ts:435-443` ≡ `supabase/functions/connector-hub/index.ts:1526-1534`.

Important correction to my own first read: connector-hub does NOT re-implement the helpers — `index.ts:81-84` imports them from `../_shared/adapterTemplates.ts`. What is duplicated is the ~20-line sequence built on top of them. `connector-hub`'s `runTemplateOp` (index.ts:1513+) and `_shared`'s `renderAction` (:429+) both perform the same ordered pipeline: seed `dateValues(new Date())` first then overlay tenant vars, render base URL, render path with `urlEncode=true`, loop `query_params` accumulating `missing`, conditionally `renderBody` for POST, filter `missing` down to real ones, then merge per-op headers BEFORE auth headers.

connector-hub is the largest file in the repo at 7,375 lines and carries 93 duplicated lines total by my per-file count — the highest of any unguarded file.
all.why_it_matters: There are two places that turn a customer's connector configuration into an actual outbound HTTP request — one for read operations, one for actions — and they were written by copying rather than sharing. The ordering rules inside are load-bearing and subtle: tenant variables must beat framework date defaults, and per-operation headers must merge before auth headers so a connector definition can never overwrite the Authorization header. That second rule is a security property, and it currently holds in both copies because someone wrote it twice correctly. The shared file's own comment says the point of `renderAction` is that preview and execute 'can never drift' — the same argument applies to this third copy, which sits outside that guarantee. Higher effort than the others because the two pipelines have genuinely different return shapes, so this is a real refactor, not a lift-and-shift.

- `supabase/functions/knowledge-gap-detect/index.ts:33` — `const DEMO_TENANT_ID = '...'`
- `supabase/functions/learned-behavior-detect/index.ts:30` — `const DEMO_TENANT_ID = '...'`
- `scripts/sql/cleanup_empty_test_tenants.sql:44` — `v_demo constant uuid := '...'; -- never touch`

The two edge copies sit inside an 18-line block my detector flagged as identical between those two files (`knowledge-gap-detect:33-56` ≡ `learned-behavior-detect:30-53`). Note the frontend one IS exported, so the two edge functions are re-declaring a constant that already has a canonical home.
all.why_it_matters: A single magic identifier written out four times, once in a cleanup script whose comment reads 'never touch'. The frontend already exports it as a named constant; the two server functions ignore that and re-type the raw string. It is a small thing, but it is the kind of value where a typo in one copy is invisible — the code runs, it just silently operates on no tenant or the wrong one, and one of the four copies governs what a deletion script refuses to delete. Cheap to fix, and the two edge copies would collapse naturally if the shared 18-line preamble they sit in were factored out.

all.title: Four writeback tables and three activity tables are byte-for-byte the same table with one column swapped
all.evidence: Column-set Jaccard over information_schema.columns for all 285 tables. account_writeback_requests / continuity_writeback_requests / invoice_writeback_requests / opportunity_writeback_requests share 14 IDENTICAL columns (applied_at, composed, created_at, created_by, de_id, decided_at, id, objective_id, op, request_summary, result, status, task_id, tenant_id) and differ ONLY by which single FK they carry: account_id / (none) / invoice_id / opportunity_id. Column-Jaccard 0.88-0.93. All four have 0 rows (query_to_xml exact count). Same pattern one level down: account_activities / invoice_activities / opportunity_activities share 8 identical columns (created_at, de_id, detail, id, kind, objective_id, summary, tenant_id), differ only by account_id / invoice_id / opportunity_id, all 0 rows. Carrying cost measured via pg_policies/pg_index: the writeback family carries 4 RLS policies + 8 indexes, the activities family 3 policies + 6 indexes. Duplication has already propagated into SQL: pg_proc scan (sql/12_routinerefs.sql) shows 4+3+3+4 = 14 separate routines for the writeback family and 2+1+2 = 5 for the activities family.
all.why_it_matters: Every new business object you support — the next one after account, invoice and opportunity — currently costs a new table, a new RLS policy, two new indexes and three or four new database routines, all copies of code that already exists. Seven tables and nineteen routines are doing the work of two tables. Because none of them has ever held a row, this is the cheapest moment there will ever be to collapse them; the cost of leaving it grows with every object type you add.

all.title: Nine business concepts exist as two or three competing tables, and the live one is not the obvious one
all.evidence: Prefixed-twin scan across all 285 table names, with exact row counts from query_to_xml. conversations(3r) / de_conversations(455r) / workforce_conversations(0r); messages(6r) / de_messages(905r); exceptions(11r) / de_exceptions(19r); knowledge_docs(2005r) / platform_knowledge_docs(65r); knowledge_chunks(0r) / knowledge_doc_chunks(5035r) / platform_knowledge_chunks(276r); usage_metrics(73r) / tenant_usage_metrics(0r); compliance_packs(3r) / tenant_compliance_packs(6r); platform_config(34r) / platform_runtime_config(2r); audit_logs(3r) / audit_events(59382r). The exceptions pair is the sharpest case: BOTH are live (11 rows and 19 rows) and each is referenced by its own routines (2 and 6 respectively per sql/12_routinerefs.sql). I verified the legacy conversations table is at least no longer written: sql/13_convrefs.sql returned inserts_conversations=false and updates_conversations=false for all four matching routines, and the four matches proved to be prose in a message string and a comment, not table access.
all.why_it_matters: When two tables have almost the same name and one holds 455 rows while the other holds 3, anyone — human or AI — writing new code has a coin-flip chance of picking the dead one. Nothing errors. The write succeeds, the row lands in the wrong table, and the feature silently shows nothing. audit_logs versus audit_events is the one to worry about most: a compliance query pointed at the 3-row table instead of the 59,382-row one would report a clean history that does not exist.

all.title: Ninety of 285 tables have never held a row, yet they carry 27% of the security rules and 29% of the indexes
all.evidence: Exact count(*) via query_to_xml across all 285 public base tables: 90 have exactly 0 rows (31.6%). Full distribution: 90 at zero, 95 with 1-9 rows, 60 with 10-99, 35 with 100-999, 5 with 1000+. So 185 of 285 tables (65%) hold fewer than 10 rows. Census via pg_policies / pg_index / pg_trigger: the 90 empty tables carry 101 of 379 RLS policies (27%), 223 of 763 indexes (29%), and 35 of 278 triggers (13%). Reachability split for those 90 (comment-stripped access-shaped matcher): 34 are wired into app code but have never been written to, 52 are reachable only via SQL routines, 4 are reachable from nowhere. Most-wired-yet-empty: eval_batch_jobs (10 edge-function sites), connector_actions (6), connector_ingest_candidates (6), connector_objects (6), commercial_agreements (5), voice_messages (5).
all.why_it_matters: More than a quarter of the access-control surface guards data that does not exist. Those 101 RLS policies have never been exercised against a real row, so their correctness is unproven — the first row written to any of these tables is also the first live test of its security rule. It also means the schema badly overstates what the product actually does: someone reading the database would conclude 285 features ship, when the evidence supports about 100.

all.title: created_by and updated_by are modelled on 67 table-columns and populated 24 times in the entire database
all.evidence: sql/09_crosscut.sql, exact counts via query_to_xml. created_by: present on 55 tables; of the 34 that contain rows, 25 are 100% NULL; total non-null created_by values across the ENTIRE database = 23. updated_by: present on 12 tables; of the 4 that contain rows, 3 are 100% NULL; total non-null values database-wide = 1. account_id: present on 21 tables, 6 of the 16 populated ones are 100% NULL, 154 values total. IMPORTANT COUNTER-EVIDENCE that changes the reading: sql/10b_audit.sql shows audit_events holds 59,382 rows with actor 100% filled across 79 distinct actors, current to today. So provenance IS captured — just not in these columns.
all.why_it_matters: This is redundant modelling, not a governance hole — I checked before concluding, and the real audit trail is healthy. The danger is narrower but sharper: 55 tables advertise a created_by column that is almost always NULL, so any future report, permission check or 'who did this' screen built on it will return blank and look like a data problem rather than a design one. The column promises an answer the schema never intended to store.

all.title: 230 columns are 100% NULL, but only 43 are genuinely dead — the rest are working UI fields nobody has filled in
all.evidence: Exact count(col) via query_to_xml over all 1,153 nullable columns in public base tables: 230 are 100% NULL in a table that HAS rows, spread across 93 tables. Stratified by table size so the claim is not built on 2-row tables: 126 dead columns sit in tables with >=10 rows, 67 in tables with >=50 rows. Split by comment-stripped grep of src/ + supabase/functions/: 43 truly dead (name absent from all app code), 132 wired-but-unused, 55 generic names not attributable by grep. Top offender profiles: 21 rows, 15 dead columns (employee_number, employment_type, end_date, hire_date, job_title, last_seen_at, locale, middle_name, mobile_phone, preferred_name, pronouns, reports_to_user_id, time_zone, work_location, work_phone) — yet job_title has a live editable input at src/components/EmployeeProfileDrawer.tsx:159-160. Next: de_conversations 455r/8 dead, human_tasks 413r/6 dead, knowledge_docs 2005r/6 dead.
all.why_it_matters: The headline number is misleading and I nearly reported it as-is: most of these are not junk to delete but finished features starved of data — the employee-profile form works, no one has typed into it. The real cost is that you cannot tell the two apart by looking. Anyone cleaning up the schema has to check each column against the UI first, so a job that sounds like an afternoon is actually 230 individual judgement calls.

all.title: The rollback path on action_executions has never once been used
all.evidence: action_executions holds 186 rows. Its three rollback columns — rollback_of, rollback_receipt, rolled_back_at — are all 100% NULL (exact count(col) via query_to_xml). Independently, none of the three column names appears anywhere in src/ or supabase/functions/ under comment-stripped grep, placing all three in the 'truly dead' bucket rather than the 'wired but unused' bucket. Same pattern on de_deployment_stages (12 rows, rollback_reason 100% NULL).
all.why_it_matters: 186 actions have been executed and not one has ever been rolled back — and the undo machinery is not merely unused, it is unreferenced by any code that could invoke it. For a product whose pitch is governed, reversible AI action-taking, the reverse gear exists on the schema diagram and nowhere else. If a digital employee does something wrong today, nothing in this database is positioned to undo it.

all.title: Eight to ten tables exist that nothing anywhere can reach
all.evidence: Cross of two independent scans: comment-stripped access-shaped grep over src/ + supabase/functions/, and comment-stripped access-shaped scan of all 890 routines, 5 views, 278 triggers and 379 policies (sql/15_strictrefs.sql). Loose matching yields 8 unreachable tables, strict matching 10 — a tight and consistent range. Both sets contain: commercial_catalog_items(4r), analytics_query_defs(2r), unguarded_secdef_writers(2r), benchmark_samples(1r), connector_sync_cursors(0r), de_channels(0r), extraction_templates(0r), knowledge_tags(0r). Verified independently with ripgrep over supabase/migrations: each appears in only 1-2 migration files, i.e. the CREATE TABLE and nothing else. connector_sync_cursors' single code hit is a comment at supabase/functions/connector-hub/index.ts:1692 reading 'paging the rest via connector_sync_cursors is the deferred follow-up'.
all.why_it_matters: This is the good news dressed as a finding: on a 285-table schema, only eight to ten tables are true orphans, and four of them still hold a handful of rows from a one-off experiment. It is the smallest category in this report and the easiest to clear. I am listing it mainly so the number is on record — the schema does not have an orphan problem.

all.title: 94 of 772 app-authored routines (12.2%) have no caller anywhere — 109 KB of orphaned database logic
all.evidence: Method: dumped every non-extension routine in `public` (772 rows, `pg_depend deptype='e'` excluded) with DB-internal reachability flags, then cross-referenced against every call site in src/, supabase/functions/, scripts/. Scripts: C:\Users\SPECTRE\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\D--Dream-Team-AI\9e864d5e-6118-4763-aad0-aba6670c7478\scratchpad\q\06_reach.sql and xref2.mjs. A routine counts as LIVE if bound to a trigger, named in another routine's prosrc, in an RLS policy, a view, a DDL expression, a cron command, or appearing in a string literal in non-comment application code. Output: {total: 772, db_reachable: 327, string_literal_callsite: 429, DEAD_strict_no_callsite: 94, dead_strict_secdef: 92}. Dead bodies total 109,303 bytes. 83 of the 94 are not mentioned outside migrations AT ALL; the remaining 11 appear only inside comments — I hand-verified every one of those 11 with `grep -rn <name> src supabase/functions scripts`, e.g. src/lib/digitalEmployeesApi.ts:269 reads `// transfer_de_ownership (DB) still exists, but its frontend wrapper is gone —`. Largest offenders: detect_exceptions (7,514 B), resolve_jit_membership (4,998), decide_inquiry_triage (4,961), ingest_document (4,785), install_role_watchers (4,565), reconcile_invoice_payments (3,323), propose_invoice_from_agreement (3,113), get_tenant_details (2,968), upsert_action_definition (2,963), calculate_tenant_monthly_cost (2,636).
all.why_it_matters: An eighth of the database's custom logic is code nobody runs. Every future security sweep, permissions audit, type regeneration and schema review has to read, reason about and re-secure it — that cost is paid on every pass, forever, for zero product value. It also actively misleads: an engineer or an audit reading `reconcile_invoice_payments` reasonably assumes invoice reconciliation is wired up, when nothing calls it.

all.title: The security gate has frozen an API surface that is 10% dead — 62 uncalled routines are pinned as permanently callable
all.evidence: D:\Dream Team AI\scripts\certify.mjs:34 sets ALLOWLIST_FILE = 'supabase/baseline/execute-allowlist.json'; lines 72-101 pin the anon/authenticated EXECUTE surface and fail certify on ANY diff in either direction (line 100: 'allowlisted grant VANISHED (revoked or fn dropped)'). Joining that pin file against my dead list: pinned_at 2026-08-08T20:03:52.572Z, 629 pinned routines, of which 62 are dead — apply_config_template, audit_chain_head, calculate_tenant_monthly_cost, certify_digital_employee, detect_exceptions, export_tenant_config, get_all_tenants_with_summary, get_tenant_details, ingest_document, is_feature_enabled, match_doc_chunks, resolve_jit_membership, sso_login_compliance, transfer_de_ownership, update_tenant_billing, update_tenant_features, upsert_action_definition, … (62 total). Separately measured: 464 of 772 routines are SECURITY DEFINER *and* EXECUTE-able by `authenticated`; 66 are EXECUTE-able by `anon`.
all.why_it_matters: The gate does its job — it stops NEW holes opening. But because it fails on removal as well as addition, it has cemented the dead surface: deleting an uncalled routine now breaks the build until someone deliberately re-pins. The safety mechanism has quietly become the reason the cleanup never happens, and one in ten published endpoints is code no part of the product calls.

all.title: 91% of routines are SECURITY DEFINER — every access check is hand-rolled, with no systemic enforcement
all.evidence: 01_counts.sql over pg_proc/pg_namespace: public schema has 885 functions + 4 aggregates + 1 procedure = 890 routines, of which 703 functions are prosecdef. Excluding the 118 extension-owned routines (03_app_owned.sql): {app_routines: 772, security_definer: 704, distinct_names: 771} → 704/772 = 91.2%. Of those, 464 are also EXECUTE-able by `authenticated`. Spot-reading bodies (14_guards.sql) confirms the guard is written by hand and differs per routine: get_tenant_details opens `IF NOT is_platform_admin() THEN RAISE EXCEPTION 'Unauthorized'`, is_feature_enabled uses `resolve_platform_capability(auth.uid(),'tenants.view') or exists(select 1 from profiles …)`, compute_account_health uses `coalesce(auth.role(),'') <> 'service_role'`, is_ancestor_of uses `caller_has_tenant_relationship(...)`. Four different guard idioms across four routines.
all.why_it_matters: SECURITY DEFINER means the routine runs with the owner's privileges and bypasses row-level security — so for 704 routines the ONLY thing standing between a logged-in user and other tenants' data is a hand-written IF at the top of each body. There is no shared guard primitive and no gate that checks one is present. A single routine shipped without its check is a cross-tenant breach, and nothing in the build would notice. This is the single biggest structural liability in the routine layer.

all.title: `decide_inquiry_triage` is a 4,961-byte dead twin of the live `decide_work_item_triage`
all.evidence: Near-duplicate detection over 706 normalized bodies using 5-gram token shingles (dup.mjs): top non-identical pair is `decide_work_item_triage(4873) <-> decide_inquiry_triage(4961,DEAD)` at Jaccard 0.771. Reachability: decide_work_item_triage → code=1, live; decide_inquiry_triage → routine=0 cron=0 code=0, DEAD. The only two repo mentions of the dead one are comments, and supabase/functions/specialist-consult/index.ts:696 names the relationship outright: `//      sibling of decide_inquiry_triage: guardrail-always-wins, then`. It is still referenced by 16 migration files, most recently 459_trust_unbrick_registered_actions.sql.
all.why_it_matters: Two 5 KB near-identical triage decision routines exist and only one runs. Any future change to triage rules has a coin-flip chance of being applied to the dead copy — the change appears to ship, tests touching the live path stay green, and behaviour never changes. This is exactly the failure mode that wastes a day and ends in 'but I DID fix it'.

all.title: The `*_writeback` family is 10 copy-pasted routines (~31 KB) differing only by entity — and one member is already dead
all.evidence: dup.mjs clustering (Jaccard >= 0.55) produced 21 clusters covering 49 routines and 84,055 bytes. Three of those clusters are the same family: propose_account_writeback(5512) / propose_continuity_writeback(5390) / propose_opportunity_writeback(5231) / propose_invoice_writeback(4558); resolve_opportunity_writeback(1279) / resolve_continuity_writeback(1274) / resolve_account_writeback(1249); apply_account_writeback_internal(2254) / apply_opportunity_writeback_internal(2131) / apply_invoice_writeback_internal(1936). Total 30,814 bytes across 10 routines. The family is asymmetric: `resolve_invoice_writeback` (747 B) is DEAD (routine=0 cron=0 code=0) while its three resolve_* siblings are live, and there is no `resolve_*` for the invoice path at all in the live set.
all.why_it_matters: Adding an eleventh entity type means hand-copying three more routines; fixing a bug in the writeback logic means finding and fixing it ten times. The asymmetry is the proof this already fails — the invoice path is missing the resolve step its siblings have, and nothing flagged that gap. Copy-paste families drift silently, and the drift shows up as one entity type behaving differently from the rest.

all.title: Dead routines are still consuming engineering effort — one was re-secured at migration 636 of 651
all.evidence: churn.mjs / churn2.mjs indexed all 672 migration files. The 94 dead routines are named across 232 migration files. Excluding timestamp-named migrations, 19 dead routines were last touched by a sequential migration >= 500 (highest sequential is 651), and 3 at >= 600. Worst case: `install_role_watchers` (4,565 B, dead) — 5 migrations, last touched at 636_cross_tenant_write_holes.sql. `grep -n install_role_watchers supabase/migrations/636_cross_tenant_write_holes.sql` shows it being re-secured at lines 55, 73 and 86, and line 29 states plainly: `-- install_role_watchers is called only from migrations and provisioning, both`. Also recently touched: get_tenant_details and update_tenant_features (mig 624), get_all_tenants_with_summary / list_kpi_metrics / save_de_config (mig 559).
all.why_it_matters: This is the compounding cost made visible. Security hardening passes are spending real effort locking down functions that nothing calls — migration 636 even documents that the routine has no application caller, and secures it anyway rather than dropping it. Every sweep re-pays this, and the bill grows with each new dead routine.

all.title: One app-authored function overload remains: `get_de_config`
all.evidence: 04_app_overloads.sql (extension functions excluded via pg_depend deptype='e') returned exactly one row: `get_de_config`, n=2, signatures `(p_de_id uuid)  |  (p_tenant_id uuid, p_entity_kind text, p_entity_id uuid)`. For contrast, the unfiltered query (02_overloads.sql) returned 13 names — the other 12 are all pgvector (array_to_vector, cosine_distance, l2_distance, l2_normalize, subvector, …). Both get_de_config signatures appear in the certify EXECUTE allowlist.
all.why_it_matters: Overloaded routine names are what caused a live outage here before (Postgres error 42725, 'function is not unique'). The good news is the class is 99% eliminated — this is the last one. The two signatures use entirely different parameter names, so PostgREST can currently tell them apart; the risk is that a future third signature, or a caller passing a partial argument set, reintroduces the ambiguity. Worth closing precisely because it is the only one left.

all.title: `sync_de_department` and `sync_profile_department` are byte-identical after normalization
all.evidence: 13_dupbodies.sql grouped 706 bodies by md5 of the comment-and-whitespace-normalized source; exactly ONE group had count > 1: `sync_de_department == sync_profile_department` (856 and 852 raw bytes). dup.mjs independently scored the pair at Jaccard 1.0. Both are trigger functions and both are bound to live triggers (bound_to_trigger=1 for each), firing on different tables.
all.why_it_matters: Two triggers on two different tables run logic that is character-for-character the same. A department-sync rule change has to be made twice, and if it is made once the two tables silently diverge — profiles saying one thing about a person's department and digital employees saying another. Small, but it is the only exact duplication in the whole 706-body corpus, so it is cheap to eliminate.

all.title: `p_workspace_period_end` is a function accidentally named after a parameter
all.evidence: 16_odd.sql returned the full body: `SELECT period_end FROM public.close_workspaces WHERE id=p_workspace_id;` — 75 bytes, signature `(p_workspace_id uuid)`, returns date, SECURITY DEFINER, dead (no caller in DB or repo), not granted to authenticated or anon. It is named with the `p_` prefix this codebase reserves for parameters. Referenced by 3 migrations, last at 040. Neighbouring oddity in the same dead set: `get_user_id_by_email(p_email text)`, 74 bytes, SECURITY DEFINER, body `select id from auth.users where lower(email) = lower(p_email) limit 1;` — an uncalled helper that reads the auth.users table.
all.why_it_matters: A function called `p_workspace_period_end` is almost certainly a typo that got committed and then survived 600+ migrations because nothing ever forced a review of the routine inventory. It is harmless on its own; it matters as evidence that routines can be created by accident here and nothing ever notices. `get_user_id_by_email` in the same dead set is the sharper version of that point — an uncalled SECURITY DEFINER function that reads the authentication table.

all.title: Zero automated tests cover any screen — 73,790 lines of UI, 0 component tests
all.evidence: `grep -rln "src/components\|src/pages" tests/ | wc -l` → 0. `ls tests/` → 11 .test.ts files (approval-learning-capture, confidence-parity, continuity-format, contract-parity, google-ads-template, knowledge-acl-invariants, marketing-adapters, response-window, tenant-isolation, write-bindings) — none import a component or page. `node -e "console.log(require('./package.json').devDependencies)"` → no @testing-library/*, no jsdom, no happy-dom. src line count: `Get-ChildItem src -Recurse -Include *.ts,*.tsx | Measure-Object -Line` → 73,790 lines across 201 files.
all.why_it_matters: Every visual or behavioural regression in the product's entire user-facing surface can only be caught by a person clicking. There is no safety net under the screens where customers approve money, grant permissions, and read what their digital employees did. The one place the codebase invests heavily in verification (certify, drift gates, DB tests) stops at the browser.

all.title: No linter exists, yet 22 places in the code suppress a lint rule that nothing runs
all.evidence: No eslint config at repo root (`ls -a | grep -i eslint` → none); eslint absent from package.json dependencies and devDependencies; `ls node_modules/.bin/ | grep -i eslint` → not installed. Meanwhile `grep -rn "eslint-disable" src/ | wc -l` → 26, of which `grep -rn "exhaustive-deps" src/ | wc -l` → 22. Example: src/App.tsx:156 `}, [currentPage, location.pathname, authedUser]); // eslint-disable-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps`.
all.why_it_matters: React's stale-data bug class (a screen showing yesterday's numbers because a dependency was forgotten) is exactly what the react-hooks rule catches. 22 places have consciously waved it off — but there is no checker behind the wave-off, so a NEW forgotten dependency produces no warning at all. The suppressions are decorative and read, misleadingly, as evidence a checker is watching.

all.title: One page file has grown to 4,414 lines holding ~30 separate panels, 190 pieces of state and 24 direct database calls
all.evidence: `Get-ChildItem src -Recurse | Measure-Object -Line` → src/pages/tenant/LiveWorkforceDEs.tsx = 4,414 lines (next largest non-generated: LivePlaybookBuilder.tsx 2,024). `grep -c useState` → 190; `grep -c useEffect` → 26; `grep -c "\.rpc("` → 24; `grep -n "^\(export \)\?\(function\|const\) [A-Z]"` → 45 top-level declarations. Largest internal component DeTrustAutonomySection ≈362 lines. src/pages/tenant/LiveWorkforceDEs.tsx:2166 `DeKpisPanel` declares 12 useState and calls `supabase.rpc('get_de_kpi_status')` inline in the rendering component.
all.why_it_matters: This is the digital-employee management screen — the product's centrepiece. Any change to it means loading 4,400 lines into working memory, and two people cannot safely work on different panels at once because they are in the same file. It is also the only page that reaches past the data-access layer straight into the database 24 times, so its query behaviour is invisible to the shared API layer everything else uses.

all.title: The design system is LAW on paper but supplies under a quarter of the buttons — and the drift gate does not measure that
all.evidence: `grep -rh "<button" src/ --include='*.tsx' --exclude-dir=design | grep -v '^[[:space:]]*\(//\|\*\)' | wc -l` → 653 raw. `grep -rh "<Button"` same filters → 195. Inputs: 329 raw `<input` vs 125 references to the kit's INPUT_CLS. Tables: 50 raw `<table` vs 9 `<TableScroll>`. Adoption by file: 62 of 128 .tsx files import src/design/primitives. `node scripts/design-drift.mjs` → 8 metrics tracked (bg-slate, border-slate, radius, card padding, StatCard-likes, hand-rolled dialogs, inline styles, raw hex) — none of them counts button/input/table primitive adoption.
all.why_it_matters: A fix made once in the kit (a focus ring, a disabled state, a touch target) reaches roughly one control in four. The rest have to be found and edited by hand, which is how screens drift apart visually. The gate that is supposed to enforce the system watches cosmetic tokens and passes green while the biggest adoption gap goes uncounted — so 'no drift regressions' overstates how much is actually under control. Caveat: some raw buttons are legitimately bespoke (nav rows, tab strips, whole-card buttons), so 653 is an upper bound, not 653 defects.

all.title: The whole app ships as one 2.1 MB JavaScript file, and the size warning has been turned off
all.evidence: dist/assets (build dated 2026-08-05): single `index-91224d7a.js` = 2,114.5 KB plus `index-d99de113.css` = 72 KB — no other chunks. vite.config.ts sets `chunkSizeWarningLimit: 5000` (Vite's default is 500). `grep -rc "React.lazy" src/` → exactly 1 file (src/main.tsx:40, a dev-only design gallery behind `import.meta.env.DEV`). `grep -c "^import .* from './pages" src/App.tsx` → 41 eagerly imported page modules.
all.why_it_matters: Every visitor downloads all 67 screens — platform console, playbook builder, connector hub — before the login box appears. On a phone or a poor connection that is the first impression. The warning that would have flagged this was raised tenfold in the build config, so the number will keep growing silently. Note: the bundle figure comes from a dist/ folder built 4 days ago; the source has moved since, so treat 2.1 MB as a floor.

all.title: A legacy compatibility shim still fronts the design kit for 30 files, and its own comment reports the wrong number
all.evidence: src/components/ui.tsx is 8 lines and re-exports `InHubContextV2 as InHubContext, PageHeaderV2 as PageHeader, TH as th` from design/primitives plus a local `td`. Its header comment claims '37 call sites keep importing from here'; `grep -rl "components/ui'" src/ --include='*.tsx' | wc -l` → 30. Only ONE file imports the real name directly (src/pages/tenant/systems/LivePlaybookBuilder.tsx:6, aliased back to PageHeader). src/components/Modal.tsx is a second such adapter (11 lines wrapping the kit's Modal) and is still re-exported from src/components/index.ts:4.
all.why_it_matters: Two names for the same thing means new work has to guess which is current, and a stale count in the comment means the migration's own progress tracker is wrong. all.title: CI and the declared runtime floor are Node 20, which passed end-of-life 101 days ago

all.title: The repo has its own security gate, it fails today, and nothing runs it

all.title: Vite is 4 majors behind with no patch path — clearing its 2 high-severity advisories requires jumping 4→8

all.title: Two different major versions of Vite in one tree: tests run on Vite 8, production builds on Vite 4
all.evidence: MEASURED. Parsed package-lock.json for packages installed at more than one tree location. Four exist, and the significant one is vite: `node_modules/vite = 4.5.14` (what `npm run build` uses, via vercel.json `"buildCommand": "npm run build"`) versus `node_modules/vitest/node_modules/vite = 8.1.3` (what `npm run test`, `test:unit`, `test:isolation`, `test:invariants` all use). vitest 4.1.10 is fully up to date and pulls Vite 8; the app is pinned to Vite 4. A green test run is weaker evidence than it looks: code can transform correctly under Vite 8's pipeline and differently under Vite 4's, so a passing suite does not prove the shipped bundle behaves the same way. This is a quiet one — it will never announce itself, it will just mean a test passed for a build that was never produced.

all.title: 56 of 60 edge functions import from deno.land, a host that now redirects to JSR, pinned to a 2022-era standard library
all.evidence: MEASURED. `grep -rho "deno.land/std@[0-9.]*"` across supabase/functions gives exactly two pins: 55 files on `deno.land/std@0.168.0` and 1 file on `deno.land/std@0.177.0` (supabase/functions/de-mission/index.ts — a lone straggler). MIT license.` There is no vendored copy and no lockfile (see finding 1), so these are fetched live at deploy.
all.why_it_matters: Fifty-six of your sixty server-side functions boot by downloading a file from a domain whose front page now redirects somewhere else, at a version last touched in 2022. The old URLs still work today. If they ever stop — a sunset, an outage, a policy change at that host — 56 functions fail to start simultaneously and there is no cached or vendored copy to fall back on. This is a concentration risk on a single external host that nobody chose deliberately; it accumulated one copy-pasted import at a time.

all.title: No dependency-update automation of any kind

The reason 9 packages drifted a full major behind is not neglect of a warning — there was never a warning. This is the cheapest structural fix available and it is what stops the report you are reading from needing to be run by hand again next quarter.

all.title: Two competing HTTP-server idioms coexist across the edge layer
all.evidence: MEASURED. 56 function directories import the standard-library shim (`import { serve } from 'https://deno.land/std@0.168.0/http/server.ts'`). It means a developer writing function 61 has to guess, and it means the fix for the deno.land concentration risk above is already half-built and half-abandoned. The four native ones are the pattern that has no external dependency.

all.title: A type-only pin freezes 6 edge functions' Supabase client types at 2.45.4 while they run ~2.112
all.evidence: MEASURED. supabase/functions/_shared/modelCall.ts:22 reads `import type { SupabaseClient } from 'https://esm.sh/@supabase/supabase-js@2.45.4';` — I confirmed via grep that this is the ONLY supabase-js import in that file, and the `import type` keyword means it is erased at runtime, so this is a type mismatch and not a runtime version conflict. Six functions import it: ai-session, compile-trust-plan, entity-amend, entity-draft, playbook-amend, playbook-draft. Their actual runtime client comes from the floating `@2` (2.112.2 today) — roughly 67 minor releases of API drift from the shape they are type-checked against. Compounding it, per the house's own record `tsc` excludes supabase/functions entirely, so this type is never checked by the build in the first place.
all.why_it_matters: Six functions describe their database client using a 2024-era definition while calling a 2026-era object. Nothing fails today because the definition is never actually enforced, which is the real point: it is a safety label on a box nobody opens. Low urgency, but it is the visible tip of finding 1 — it only exists because there is no single place that says which version this project uses.

all.title: Installs use `npm install` rather than `npm ci` everywhere, including the production deploy
all.evidence: MEASURED. Five call sites, all `npm install`: .github/workflows/ci.yml lines 36, 56 and 79; .github/workflows/provision-on-deploy.yml line 28; and vercel.json line 4, `"installCommand": "npm install"` — that last one is the production build. HONEST CAVEAT, and it matters: I checked for actual drift with `npm install --dry-run` and it reported "up to date in 3s", so package.json, package-lock.json and node_modules currently agree. There is no drift right now. The gap is enforcement, not a present defect: `npm ci` fails loudly when the lockfile and manifest disagree, `npm install` silently reconciles them.
all.why_it_matters: Today this costs nothing — the lockfile happens to be in sync. But the production deploy is configured so that if it ever stops being in sync, the build quietly installs something other than what was committed and reports success. It is a missing tripwire rather than an active wound, and I want to be clear about that distinction rather than inflate it.

all.title: The documented one-command deploy cannot apply migrations — both runners call a database function that does not exist
all.evidence:
scripts/DEPLOY_SETUP.md documents `node scripts/deploy.mjs` as THE deploy command ("applies pending migrations + deploys edge functions + verifies"). Both halves of its migration path are dead against the real database.

(1) It reads the wrong ledger. scripts/deploy.mjs:70 `await sb.from('_supabase_migrations').select('name')`. Probing PostgREST with the anon key: `GET /rest/v1/_supabase_migrations?select=name&limit=1` -> `HTTP 404 {"code":"PGRST205","hint":"Perhaps you meant the table 'public.schema_migrations'","message":"Could not find the table 'public._supabase_migrations' in the schema cache"}`. The same query against `schema_migrations` returns HTTP 200. Because that read errors, `appliedMax` stays null and deploy.mjs:77 hits `die('Cannot determine applied state...')` on every run without an explicit --mig/--since.

(2) It applies SQL through a nonexistent RPC. scripts/deploy.mjs:86 `await sb.rpc('exec_sql', { sql })`. Production query `select n.nspname, p.proname from pg_proc p join pg_namespace n on n.oid=p.pronamespace where p.proname ilike '%exec_sql%'` returned `[]` — no such function in any schema.

(3) The same two defects are in `npm run migrate:apply` -> scripts/apply-migration.mjs:30, :46, :55 (which additionally builds its client from SUPABASE_ANON_KEY at :20).

The path that actually works is scripts/db-query.mjs, which posts to the Supabase Management API and then records the file via `record_migration_applied` (db-query.mjs:70). Production ledger provenance confirms it: `select provenance, count(*) ... from public.schema_migrations group by provenance` -> `applied_by_runner 304` (first 2026-07-26, last 2026-08-09), `assumed_pre_ledger 368`.
all.why_it_matters: The written-down deploy procedure and the procedure that actually works are two different things, and only one person's habit bridges the gap. Anyone new — or the same person under pressure at 2am — follows the documentation, gets an error, and starts improvising against the production database. It also means there is no single command that ships a change end to end, so "did the database part actually go out?" is answered by memory rather than by a tool.

all.title: No automated backups, the only full data export is 14 days old and excludes every user account, and no data-restore path exists
all.evidence:
backups/2026-07-26-09-23-53/_manifest.json: `exported_at 2026-07-26T09:38:15Z`, `total_rows 57033`, `vectors_omitted: true`, `not_included: ["auth.users — user accounts and credentials live in the auth schema", "storage objects", "vault secrets ...", "pg_cron schedules"]`. The only other directory, backups/outsourcetel-hq-2026-07-30/, is one tenant and has an empty `_manifest.json` (`{}`).

Nothing schedules these: `grep -n "schedule|cron" .github/workflows/*.yml` returns nothing across both workflow files. scripts/backup-data.mjs:8-13 states the Supabase org is on the FREE plan and the backups endpoint returns an empty list, so there is no platform-side backup either.

There is no restore script for data. `grep -rn restore scripts/*.mjs` finds restore only in backup-*.mjs comments and in scripts/restore-drill.mjs — and that drill is SCHEMA-only: restore-drill.mjs:32-35 restores supabase/baseline/full_schema.sql into schema `bkp_verify` on the DEV project, and its comparison (the `census` query at :126-144) compares object COUNTS — tables, views, functions, triggers, policies, rls_enabled, columns — not definitions.

That is not a backup you can run a business on. It is also a laptop-local copy of real customer PII, which is a second exposure the script's own header calls out.

all.title: The project's real quality gate — 9 sections that pass in under 3 minutes — is not in CI
all.evidence:
`grep -rn "certify|golden-path|design-drift|audit:role-gates" .github/workflows/` returns nothing. CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs exactly: `npm run build`, `npm run test:unit`, `npm run test:isolation`, `npm run test:invariants`.

`npm run test:unit` is `vitest run tests/continuity-format.test.ts` (package.json:20) — ONE file. tests/ holds 10 test files; CI names 3 of them. Not run by CI: approval-learning-capture, confidence-parity, contract-parity, google-ads-template, marketing-adapters, response-window, write-bindings.

It only fires when a human remembers to type it, on a laptop that holds production credentials. A green tick on GitHub therefore means far less than it appears to, and the day someone ships without running certify locally there is nothing to catch it.

all.title: Alerts fire correctly and reach nobody unless someone happens to be looking at a dashboard — 78 sit unresolved right now

Production: `select kind, count(*), max(created_at), count(*) filter (where resolved_at is null) from ops_alerts group by kind` returns 240 alerts across 8 kinds, of which 78 are unresolved: de_objective_wake_spin 52 (newest 2026-08-09), edge_function_error 23 (newest 2026-08-05), dispatch_failure 2 (newest 2026-08-09 13:07), ai_budget_approaching 1.

all.title: The JWT gate for 59 production edge functions exists only inside Supabase — nothing in the repo records it
all.evidence:
Management API `/v1/projects/rfsvmhcqeiyrxivbmpel/functions`: 59 deployed, 47 with `verify_jwt=false`, 12 with `verify_jwt=true`.

`find supabase -maxdepth 2 -name config.toml` returns nothing — there is no config.toml. The only record of intent in the repo is the hardcoded 4-name set at scripts/deploy.mjs:113-118 (scim, mcp-demo-server, voice-turn, voice-webhook); mcp-demo-server is not deployed, so 3 of the 47 are represented. The remaining ~44 functions' setting is stored nowhere but Supabase's own state.

The file documents the trade-off itself at deploy.mjs:103-112: introducing a config.toml would make it the source of truth and "silently flip every function it does not mention back to verify_jwt=true, which would break the anonymous widget (widget-ask), the inbound email hook, the OAuth callback and 45 others." The current mechanism is that `supabase functions deploy` with no flag preserves whatever the function already has.
all.why_it_matters: Whether a public endpoint is open or closed is decided by remote state nobody can read in a code review, and preserved only by a CLI behaviour that could change under you. Rebuilding this project from the repo — a new Supabase project, a disaster recovery, a second region — produces 44 functions gated the wrong way, and the failure is silent in one direction (a widget stops working) and dangerous in the other. It is also the single hardest thing here to reconstruct if the current project is lost.

all.title: Dev is not a smaller production — it is a divergent one, with 8 tables prod doesn't have and no active tenant at all
all.evidence:
Same census query run against both projects via scripts/db-query.mjs and scripts/dev-query.mjs.

Schema — PROD: 285 tables / 890 routines / 379 policies / 5 views. DEV: 292 / 907 / 390 / 5. Diffing table names: in DEV not in PROD — de_specialist_assignments, embed_tokens, media_assets, scribe_requests, sod_policies, spec_consultations, specialist_profiles, specialist_sources (8). In PROD not in DEV — benchmark_samples (1).

Bugs that only appear with real content — retrieval, conversation history, anything gated on an active tenant — cannot be reproduced there, and code paths that exist only in dev (8 tables' worth) can pass a check that means nothing for production.

all.title: 55% of the schema history is recorded as 'believed applied, never verified'
all.evidence:
`npm run -s migrate:status` against production (rfsvmhcqeiyrxivbmpel): "672 files in supabase/migrations, 672 in the ledger — APPLIED 304 recorded by the runner, file unchanged; ASSUMED 368 predates the ledger, believed applied, never verified; DRIFTED 0; PENDING 0; ORPHANED 0." Confirmed directly against the table: `select provenance, count(*) from public.schema_migrations group by provenance` -> assumed_pre_ledger 368, applied_by_runner 304.

The ledger itself only exists from migration 364 (supabase/migrations/364_migration_ledger.sql:38), and scripts/migration-status.mjs:67-71 backfills everything older as ASSUMED without checking.
all.why_it_matters: Rebuilding the database by replaying migrations — the fallback if the schema dump ever fails — is unproven for more than half the history. Combined with the schema backup being count-compared rather than definition-compared, there are two independent recovery routes and neither has been shown to reproduce production exactly.

all.title: The production anon key is baked into migration files, so rotating it means editing history
all.evidence:
`git grep -n eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs -- supabase` hits supabase/migrations/119_dispatch_cron_jwt_fix.sql:27 (`v_anon text := 'eyJ...'`), supabase/migrations/161_de_work_cron.sql:19, and 8 sites in supabase/baseline/full_schema.sql. Those dispatch functions are what 49 active pg_cron jobs invoke.

Partially mitigated: the baseline occurrences are `coalesce((select value from platform_runtime_config where key = 'supabase_anon_key'), 'eyJ...')` — config first, literal as fallback (the mechanism scripts/set-runtime-config.mjs:4-11 describes, added in migration 383). Migrations 119 and 161 have the bare literal with no config lookup.

This is not a secret leak — the anon key is public by design and already ships in the browser bundle.
all.why_it_matters: If that key ever has to be rotated — a compromise, a project move, a Supabase-side change — the scheduled jobs that run the whole digital workforce keep presenting the old one from a hardcoded fallback, and the symptom is queues quietly not draining rather than a visible error.

all.title: No README, no index, no way in — 140 docs with no front door
all.evidence: `ls README* readme*` at repo root → "No such file or directory". `ls docs/ | grep -i -E "index|readme|start|contents|00"` → only the directory `32-pre-start-reports`; no index file. `git ls-files "docs/*.md" | wc -l` → 140.
